title: Why Random Darts Beat Grids in 100 Dimensions

beats.text: Your budget: a million evaluations to average a function of a hundred inputs. [pause 0.25] Spread them out as an even grid; that feels thorough. [pause 0.2] How many values does each input get? [pause 1.5]
One. [pause 0.2] The whole grid is one point, the centre of the box. [pause 0.2] Two values per input would take two to the hundredth points. [pause 0.8]

Pricing an option on a hundred stocks is this kind of average. [pause 0.2] Since Metropolis and Ulam's 1949 paper, such averages are usually done with random points, like this one. [pause 0.25] How far off would a million of them land? [pause 0.15] Hold that thought.
Start with two inputs: a square. [pause 0.2] Our function is one inside this quarter disc, zero outside, so its average is the disc's share: exactly one half.
A ten by ten grid puts fifty-two of its hundred points inside: two points off.
A hundred random darts put forty-four inside: six points off. [pause 0.25] In two dimensions, the grid wins.
Now give each a million points, and add inputs. [pause 0.2] The disc becomes a ball that always covers exactly half the box.
The grid splits its million across the axes: a thousand values per axis in two dimensions, then a hundred, ten, three.
From twenty dimensions on, just one: the centre, which sits inside the ball. [pause 0.15] So the grid says the ball fills the box: fifty points off.
Even two values on nineteen of the axes, half a million points, is eighteen points off. [pause 0.25] The darts stay under a tenth of a point in every dimension.
Look at the shadows on one axis: the grid's hundred points cast ten, a hundred darts cast a hundred.
With N points over d axes, [pause 0.4] each axis gets the d-th root of N. [pause 0.3]
But shadows alone are not the fix. [pause 0.15] A million points on the diagonal, each one a flat line here, give every axis a million values, and still miss by eight points. [pause 0.6]
Darts win another way: each one lands inside with a chance equal to the answer, on its own, in two dimensions or a hundred. [pause 0.2] Their estimate is a share of heads in N coin flips.
One flip is zero or one. [pause 0.15] Its average is a half, and every flip misses that by exactly a half.

Repeat the hundred-dart experiment three hundred times. [pause 0.2] In two dimensions the estimates spread this wide; in a hundred, just as wide. [pause 0.25] Quadruple the darts, and both get twice as narrow.

Each dart misses by a half, up or down at random, so the misses partly cancel: sixteen darts stray about four halves, not sixteen. [pause 0.25] N darts stray about root N halves; per dart, that's a half over the square root of N. [pause 0.8]
Any other function swaps that half for its own spread, sigma. [pause 0.6] The root N stays, and there's no d in it. [pause 0.2] A grid's error, even for smooth functions, has d in its exponent.

So, back to our ball, with a million darts, in any dimension: how far off is a typical estimate? [pause 1.5] One half over a thousand: five hundredths of a point. [pause 0.8] Two runs in three land closer; all six of ours did.

In 2012, Bergstra and Bengio found that random search tuned neural networks as well as grid search, in a fraction of the time. [pause 0.2] If one setting matters most, nine grid trials test three values of it; nine random trials test nine.

Darts do have a blind spot: tiny answers. [pause 0.2] By thirty dimensions, a radius-one ball fills two parts in a hundred trillion of the box. [pause 0.2] Below this line, a million darts expect under one hit, so they usually report zero: off by the whole answer.
The darts never noticed the axes: [pause 0.3] a million coin flips, in any dimension.
